justification: No articles were provided linking SLCO6A1 to epilepsy as of 2010/12/31. Without any literature—genetic, functional, expression, or animal model—there is no basis to support an established, existing, or even hypothesized relationship. SLCO6A1 is an organic anion transporter family member, but no evidence in the supplied set connects it to seizure biology or epilepsy patients. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel.

No article in this set reports EPHX1 variants causing or conferring susceptibility to epilepsy itself; all human genetic findings concern pharmacogenetics in patients who already have epilepsy. PMID 19620853 links EPHX1 c.337T>C and c.416A>G to carbamazepine maintenance dose, PMID 19952982 links maternal EPHX1 Y113H/H139R to phenytoin-induced craniofacial malformations, PMID 20602612 reports EPHX1 polymorphism frequencies in North Indian epilepsy patients, and PMID 19127076 describes a carbamazepine hypersensitivity case with an EPHX1 variant — these are drug-response/toxicity phenotypes, not epilepsy causation. Mechanistic/functional work (PMIDs 19364907, 15535985, 15465926) supports biological relevance through hydrolysis of antiepileptic drug epoxides, which fits a hypothesized, pathway-level link to the epilepsy context. Therefore Established is essentially excluded (no independent probands/families with causal variants), with probability split between Existing (human variant associations within epilepsy cohorts) and Hypothesized (biology/drug-metabolism relevance only).

No article reports GRM1 sequence variants or association signals in epilepsy patients; the genetic studies of GRM1 present here concern early-onset cerebellar ataxia (negative, PMID 19924463), bipolar disorder in Gypsy families (no ancestral haplotype, PMID 18444255), personality traits (negative, PMID 20464528) and taste receptor variants (PMID 19146926), none of which establish a variant–epilepsy link. The supportive evidence is biological: altered mGluR1 immunoreactivity in hippocampi of patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (PMID 11951051), interneuron-specific mGluR1/5 contribution to epileptiform activity in rat slices (PMID 20698876), kindling-induced upregulation of group I mGluR responses (PMID 8899650), and anticonvulsant efficacy of selective mGlu1 antagonists LY367385, AIDA and LY456236 in rodent seizure models (PMIDs 10096765, 16011839), plus reviews implicating group I mGluRs in epilepsy (PMIDs 10416961, 20632969, 19112153). This constitutes strong mechanistic/pharmacological and expression-level support without human genetic evidence, i.e., Hypothesized. A small residual probability is left for Existing in case the human tissue expression data were interpreted as a disease-linked mechanism.

None of the provided articles mention epilepsy or seizures at all; the human genetic association studies of CPLX2 concern schizophrenia and cognition (PMID 16442780, 16131404, 20819981), and the animal work concerns depression-like behaviour, Huntington's disease models, mossy fibre LTP, and a "second hit" schizophrenia model (PMIDs 20584925, 16197510, 20412316). There are no human probands or families with CPLX2 variants linked to epilepsy, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only basis for a possible relationship is indirect biology: complexin 2 modulates SNARE-dependent neurotransmitter release and hippocampal synaptic plasticity (PMIDs 16197510, 20829354, 16162394), a pathway class broadly relevant to neuronal excitability, which gives some weight to Hypothesized. However, since no article in this set links CPLX2 to epileptiform activity, seizure phenotypes, or epilepsy patients, Novel is the most defensible designation based on this literature as of 2010.

All of the evidence concerns expression and functional biology, not genetic variation. Human studies (PMIDs 17660056, 19499324, 16651883, 18247188) describe altered Bcl-2/apoptosis-pathway protein expression in resected hippocampus or neocortex of temporal lobe epilepsy patients, which is descriptive/mechanistic rather than evidence that BCL2 variants cause or confer risk for epilepsy. The remaining work is in rodents (kindling, kainate status epilepticus, Bcl-w/Bim/Puma/Mcl1 knockout mice) supporting a role for the Bcl-2 family in seizure-induced neuronal death, i.e., biologically relevant but not variant-based. No article reports BCL2 sequence variants in epilepsy probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is only marginally supportable. The gene's biology is clearly relevant to seizure-induced neurodegeneration, making Hypothesized the best fit.

Several papers report their own primary human genetic results identifying SCN1A variants in independent patient cohorts: PMID 12754708 found de novo coding mutations in nine isolated SMEI patients, PMID 12821740 identified SCN1A mutations in 33 of 93 SMEI patients (mostly de novo, some inherited from mildly affected parents), and PMID 17347258 detected mutations in 79% of SMEI and 69% of SMEB patients plus other infantile epileptic encephalopathies among 188 probands. Additional independent human evidence comes from PMID 20506560 (novel 5' promoter-region microdeletions in Dravet patients), PMID 19782004 (mutation in a Lennox-Gastaut-like patient), PMID 18021921 (segregating T1174S in a three-generation family with epilepsy/migraine phenotypes), and PMID 16525050 (R859C segregating in a 33-member GEFS+ family). Functional/electrophysiological studies (12086636, 12535936, 11422459) provide supportive mechanistic data but are not needed for the causal claim. The replication across multiple independent probands and families, with point mutations rather than multigene deletions, firmly supports "Established".

The only article directly connecting HTR2A to epilepsy is a human transcriptomic study of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (PMID 16399808), which reports consistent dysregulation of HTR2A expression in the entorhinal cortex of MTLE patients — this is expression/pathophysiology evidence, not evidence that sequence variants in HTR2A cause or associate with epilepsy. All remaining articles concern HTR2A polymorphisms in psychiatric phenotypes (schizophrenia, depression, antidepressant response, tardive dyskinesia, panic disorder, personality, obesity, Tourette syndrome, memory), none of which is a recognized precursor or risk factor for epilepsy. No case-control or family-based genetic association study of HTR2A variants with epilepsy is present, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The biological plausibility (serotonergic neurotransmission in temporal lobe epilepsy) plus human expression data place this squarely in Hypothesized.

No article in this set reports any human genetic association between CHRM2 variants and epilepsy; the human studies concern intelligence/cognition (PMID 17996044), depression (PMID 12116189), nicotine and heroin addiction (PMIDs 19644963, 19500151), externalizing psychopathology (PMID 18316677), and event-related oscillations (PMID 16823639). The only epilepsy co-mention is a mouse mapping study (PMID 10549128) where the El2 epilepsy allele was considered for Chrm5 (not Chrm2) and the hypothesis was explicitly refuted; the mouse Chrm2 mutation study (PMID 20819376) found no behavioral/physiologic phenotype and is not human evidence. The only tenuous biological basis is CHRM2's described role in neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity and cholinergic feedback (PMID 17996044) plus electrophysiological/theta oscillation effects (PMID 16823639), which could underpin a weak "hypothesized" mechanistic link but are not epilepsy-specific. Accordingly, Established is effectively excluded (no PMIDs with epilepsy patients and CHRM2 variants), and the evidence falls between Novel and a weak Hypothesized rating.

The only available evidence is a mouse study (PMID 15677329) showing that a targeted Cacng4 mutation exacerbates spike-wave absence seizures when combined with Cacng2 (stargazer) alleles, with thalamic expression within the corticothalamic circuit. This is strong biological and animal-model support for a role in seizure susceptibility, but it is entirely murine, with no human probands, families, or variant data. No human genetic association or clinical study is present in the provided literature, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. The relationship is therefore best classified as Hypothesized, and clearly not Novel given the direct seizure-modifying animal evidence.

None of the provided articles mentions epilepsy or seizures, and none reports CSNK1A1 variants in human patients with any neurological seizure phenotype. The literature here is dominated by in vitro and non-human biochemistry of casein kinase 1 isoforms (Wnt/beta-catenin, Hedgehog, p53, HIF-1, FADD, hnRNP-C, circadian FRQ/DBT) plus a myelodysplasia expression study (PMID 17916100) where CSNK1A1 is merely a 5q deletion-region gene. Neural relevance exists only indirectly: CK1 regulation of amyloid-beta production (PMID 17360493), CK1delta forebrain overexpression in mice producing hyperactivity (PMID 20145109), CK1 involvement in neuronal differentiation (PMID 20647756), and altered Csnk1a1 expression in rat ADHD models (PMID 18937310) — none of these concerns epilepsy or human CSNK1A1 variation. Therefore the relationship is essentially unsupported (Novel), with a modest allowance for a generic "brain-expressed kinase with neuronal signaling roles" biological rationale (Hypothesized).

None of the provided articles mentions epilepsy, seizures, or any neurological disease phenotype, and none reports human genetic variants in VTI1A in patients, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The literature is entirely cell-biological: VTI1A as a SNARE in Golgi/endosomal trafficking, pulmonary hypertension models, adipose adiponectin secretion, and Dictyostelium phagosome maturation. The only neurobiologically suggestive data are that a brain-specific splice variant Vti1a-beta is enriched on small synaptic vesicles and forms a novel SNARE complex (PMID 10908612), and that a VAMP7/Vti1a complex is required for surface trafficking of Kv4/KChIP A-type potassium channels (PMID 19138172) — pathways plausibly relevant to neuronal excitability, which supports a weak Hypothesized rating. Because this connection to epilepsy is inferential and never stated in the papers, Novel and Hypothesized are roughly balanced.

The central article linking KCNQ1 to epilepsy (PMID 20368164) demonstrates seizures and brain expression of KvLQT1 in mouse lines carrying human LQT1 mutations — compelling biology and an animal model, but the epilepsy phenotype itself is not demonstrated in human mutation carriers, which places it in Hypothesized. Human reports involving KCNQ1 and seizures (PMIDs 15469540, 12443809, 16969682) describe long-QT syndrome/Jervell–Lange-Nielsen patients whose convulsive episodes were cardiogenic syncope misdiagnosed as epilepsy, i.e., phenocopies rather than proven epileptogenic variants; nonetheless, these raise the possibility that KCNQ1 variation contributes to seizure phenotypes (some weight to Existing). The remaining KCNQ1 papers concern LQTS, atrial fibrillation, and deafness, while the genuine epilepsy genes in these reviews are KCNQ2/KCNQ3, with KCNQ1 mentioned only as a homolog (PMIDs 9425900, 9677360, 9827540, 11448722, 18238816). No two independent human studies report epilepsy-causing KCNQ1 variants in probands/families, so Established is essentially excluded.

No article reports pathogenic or associated variants in ACHE itself in epilepsy patients; the mutation papers (PMIDs 10665486, 18180250, 15034473) concern COLQ, the collagenic tail subunit gene, and the phenotype is congenital myasthenic syndrome, not epilepsy. The strongest support is mechanistic/animal: AChE knockout mice die from seizures and show cholinergic receptor downregulation (PMIDs 17192642, 12667913), and AChE-inhibiting organophosphates/carbamates reliably provoke status epilepticus in rodents and humans (PMIDs 11405258, 17188316, 1733053, 3063684). Human data are biochemical rather than genetic—altered serum AChE activity in epileptic patients (PMID 358006) and altered hippocampal AChE staining in temporal lobe epilepsy (PMID 2802534)—which supports biological relevance but not variant-level association. Therefore the evidence best fits "Hypothesized," with a small allowance for "Existing" based on the human enzyme-activity correlations.

None of the provided articles mentions epilepsy, seizures, or any epilepsy-related human genetic study; there are no patient cohorts, probands, or families with RPH3A variants, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded. The literature is almost entirely biochemical and cell-biological, describing rabphilin-3A as a Rab3 effector that binds SNAP-25 and regulates synaptic vesicle priming, docking, and recovery from use-dependent depression (PMID 16763567, 17156129, 11466418), with mouse Rab3A/rabphilin mutants showing behavioral and synaptic alterations (PMID 16734774). This synaptic-release biology is mechanistically relevant to neuronal excitability and thus provides a plausible, indirect hypothesis-level link to epilepsy, supporting "Hypothesized." However, since epilepsy is never addressed and the connection must be inferred entirely by the reader, substantial probability remains for "Novel" (purely incidental co-mention/no evidence). Other articles (tumor suppressor screening, pheochromocytoma secretion, STR replacements) are unrelated to epilepsy.

None of the provided articles report epilepsy or seizures in association with CPLX1, and no human genetic variant studies linking CPLX1 to epilepsy are present; the only human association study (PMID 16442780) concerns schizophrenia and was negative. The Cplx1 knockout mouse literature (PMIDs 16000319, 17652102) describes ataxia, motor, exploratory and social deficits without reported seizures, so animal data do not directly support an epilepsy phenotype. However, CPLX1 biology is highly relevant to neuronal excitability: it modulates SNARE-dependent neurotransmitter release and vesicle priming (PMID 19255244), and complexin 1/2 are markers of inhibitory versus excitatory synapses with developmentally regulated excitatory/inhibitory balance in human cortex (PMID 18240322), providing a plausible mechanistic (though indirect) link to seizure susceptibility. This supports at most a Hypothesized relationship, with substantial probability that the relationship would be judged Novel given the complete absence of epilepsy co-mention in this literature set.

Two human genetic studies report association of SYN2 variation with epilepsy: a north Indian case-control study of the intronic SNP rs3773364 in idiopathic epilepsy (PMID 20034013) and the multicentre EPIGEN candidate-gene study, in which SYN2 was among the five genes flagged by set-association analysis, though explicitly described as tentative and population-specific (PMID 17913586). These are association findings in common variants, not causal mutations segregating in probands or families, so the Established threshold is not met. Strong supporting biology comes from animal models—synapsin I/II and triple knockout mice develop seizures and cortico-hippocampal hyperexcitability (PMIDs 7777057, 20804820, 19236947, 20338242)—and from expression changes in rodent seizure models (PMIDs 18186018, 9700837), but these are non-human and only support Hypothesized. The weight therefore falls on Existing, with residual probability on Hypothesized given the weakness/limited replication of the human associations.

No human genetic study in this set reports an association between GRIK3 (GluR7) variants and epilepsy. The only human variant studied, the Ser310Ala polymorphism, is linked to schizophrenia, recurrent major depression, personality traits, and delirium tremens (PMIDs 11986986, 16958029, 19221446, 16314883); notably, the alcoholism study explicitly tested alcohol-withdrawal seizures and found no significant association, which is a negative result for a seizure phenotype. Supportive biological evidence is substantial, however: GluR7 mRNA levels are altered in human hippocampi of temporal lobe epilepsy patients (PMID 9848088), GluR7 mRNA is downregulated after kainate-induced status epilepticus in rats (PMID 15857425), KAR subunit expression correlates with kainate seizure susceptibility in Prnp-null mice (PMID 17304577), and GluR7-affine antagonists are anticonvulsant in kindling (PMID 9987029). Together these support a biologically plausible but genetically unproven relationship, i.e., Hypothesized; a small probability is retained for Existing given the human TLE expression data could be construed as weak human-level support.

The only human genetic association studies of GRM8 variants in seizure phenotypes are explicitly negative: no association of the mGluR8 2756C/T polymorphism with idiopathic generalised epilepsy (PMID 10690750) or with alcohol withdrawal seizures/delirium tremens (PMID 11912074). Other human GRM8 association reports concern alcohol dependence/theta oscillations (PMID 18618593, 18634760), depression (PMID 20800221) and autism (PMID 17955477), which are not epilepsy precursors. In contrast, there is abundant animal and in vitro evidence implicating mGluR8 biologically in seizures: selective mGluR8 agonists (S-3,4-DCPG, PPG) are anticonvulsant in DBA/2 mice, GEP rats and electroshock models (PMIDs 10556677, 11311902, 11476756, 14529950), and mGluR8-mediated presynaptic inhibition is downregulated in pilocarpine and kindling models (PMIDs 12539201, 17430409, 10428411). This constitutes strong mechanistic/animal-model support without human variant evidence, i.e., Hypothesized; no PMIDs demonstrate causal variants in patients, so Established is untenable.

All of the provided articles concern CYP3A4 as a drug-metabolizing enzyme relevant to antiepileptic drug pharmacokinetics (zonisamide, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, stiripentol, rufinamide) and drug–drug interactions, not as a susceptibility gene for epilepsy. No study reports CYP3A4 variants in epilepsy probands or families causing seizures; the only genotyping study (PMID 17376120) examined CYP3A4/CYP2C9/19 and transporter genotypes against carbamazepine/phenytoin dose requirement and found effects attributable to MDR1, not CYP3A4. Thus no "Established" evidence exists, and at best a weak pharmacogenetic rationale (variable CYP3A4 activity influencing AED levels and hence seizure control) supports biological plausibility. This fits "Hypothesized" — the gene's biology is directly relevant to epilepsy treatment and drug exposure — with residual probability for "Novel" (co-mention only, as drug metabolism is not epilepsy pathogenesis) and a small allowance for "Existing" given the pharmacogenetic framing in human patients.

No article reports sequence variants in SLC17A6 (VGLUT2) identified in epilepsy patients or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is barely supported. The strongest functional evidence is from an animal model: vGLUT2 heterozygous knockout mice show reduced thresholds for PTZ-induced myoclonic and clonic seizures (PMID 19171171), which is animal rather than human genetic evidence. Human tissue studies show altered VGLUT2 expression in epileptogenic lesions (focal cortical dysplasia balloon cells and dysplastic neurons, PMID 17711980; human lateral amygdala neurons, PMID 16214367), and rodent models of cortical dysplasia, hypoxic epilepsy, MAM exposure, and absence epilepsy report VGLUT2 expression/uptake changes (PMIDs 20477846, 16083865, 17241223, 17725845) — all expression/mechanistic, not variant-based. Biochemical work on VGLUT2 transport (PMID 17046815) supports biological plausibility via glutamatergic excitability, while the 14-3-3 trout paper is incidental. This profile fits "Hypothesized": strong biological and animal-model rationale without human genetic variant evidence.

The foundational paper claiming three causal CLCN2 mutations in IGE families (PMID 12612585) was formally retracted (PMID 19710717), removing the strongest "causal" evidence. Remaining human genetic data are suggestive but not definitive: Niemeyer et al. (PMID 19191339) found two novel missense variants with accelerated deactivation but explicitly noted incomplete segregation and transmission by unaffected parents, concluding they are at best susceptibility factors; D'Agostino et al. (PMID 15505175) and Stogmann (PMID 19200853) report rare variants of uncertain significance; Everett et al. (PMID 17580110) report only suggestive linkage/association in childhood absence epilepsy. Several studies explicitly argue against a role (PMIDs 16932951, 20037607, 19710712, 17567819, which showed prior "epilepsy" variants are likely innocuous polymorphisms), and mouse knockouts show leukoencephalopathy/neurodegeneration rather than lowered seizure threshold (PMIDs 17567819, 20116415). Because no two independent, non-retracted human studies convincingly demonstrate causality, "Existing" (limited, contested association/susceptibility evidence) is the most appropriate category, with residual weight on Hypothesized given the strong but animal/in vitro mechanistic rationale.

All direct genetic evidence linking CACNA2D2 to epilepsy comes from mouse models: the ducky, ducky2J, and entla alleles and a targeted Cacna2d2 knockout all produce spike-wave absence seizures and ataxia (PMIDs 11487633, 11756448, 14660671, 15331424, 17135419), supported by in vitro functional data on the α2δ-2 subunit (PMIDs 10766861, 10762351, 17403543). No human study reports pathogenic CACNA2D2 variants in patients; in fact, direct sequencing/linkage in consanguineous CAE families explicitly excluded CACNA2D2 (PMID 20561025). The genome-wide linkage study found a 3p23-p14 CAE locus containing CACNA2D2 as a positional candidate, but fine-mapping association was with TRAK1, not CACNA2D2 (PMID 19837565), so this does not constitute human genetic evidence for this gene. The only other human variant report (rs2236957) concerns hypertension, an unrelated phenotype. Therefore the relationship is strongly biologically plausible via animal models and function, but lacks human variant evidence: Hypothesized.

No article reports sequence variants in GLS identified in epilepsy patients or families; there is no genetic association or mutation study at all, so Established is excluded and Existing is essentially unsupported. The strongest human datum is increased phosphate-activated glutaminase (PAG/GLS) immunoreactivity and per-neuron activity in hippocampal neurons of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy patients (PMID 17115168), which is expression/functional rather than variant evidence. Supporting biology comes from animal and in vitro work: glutaminase inhibitors (DON, azaserine) protect audiogenic seizure-prone mice (PMID 6145159), glutaminase activity rises during convulsions in rat brain (PMIDs 20492947, 2577218), lead-induced seizure models show altered PAG activity (PMID 15149801), and reviews link Gln/Glu cycling and PAG to epilepsy (PMIDs 22018046, 7926). Several listed papers concern an unrelated "GlsA" gene in Volvox or "GLS" as Garcia-Lurie syndrome and are homonym/irrelevant. Hence the relationship is best described as biologically Hypothesized.

No article in this set reports a causal CHRNB4 variant identified in epilepsy patients; the only human genetic signal is a single ADNFLE family with linkage to 15q24 near the CHRNA5/A3/B4 cluster (PMID 9758605, LOD 3.01), which cannot isolate CHRNB4 from its neighbouring genes and was never followed by a mutation. Several subsequent studies explicitly excluded linkage/mutations at CHRNB4 and the whole nAChR cluster in independent ADNFLE and idiopathic epilepsy families (PMIDs 12195439, 17324557, 15597263), weakening the human evidence. The remaining support is biological and candidate-gene framing: CHRNB4 encodes a brain-expressed nAChR subunit in the same family as the proven ADNFLE genes CHRNA4/CHRNB2 (PMIDs 11721883, 9921897, 15119829), and β4-deficient mice and nicotine-induced seizure models link the subunit to seizure activity (PMIDs 16985005, 17456735). Human coding polymorphisms in β4 have been characterized functionally in oocytes but without any epilepsy phenotype association (PMID 15742216). This profile fits "Hypothesized" best, with meaningful residual probability for "Existing" based on the single suggestive linkage family.

The only direct epilepsy evidence comes from mouse knockouts: Slc17a8/VGLUT3-null mice show primary generalized, nonconvulsive seizures and altered cortical excitability (PMID 18215623, reviewed in 18215615), which is a strong but purely animal-model link. The sole human genetic finding for SLC17A8 is the missense variant p.A211V segregating with autosomal-dominant nonsyndromic deafness DFNA25 (PMID 18674745); deafness is not epilepsy nor a recognized epilepsy precursor, so this does not support "Existing." Other papers describe expression/function of VGLUT3 in brain, striatal cholinergic interneurons, zebrafish hair cells, and nigral neurons, supporting biological plausibility (modulation of excitatory/cholinergic tone) but providing no human variant–epilepsy association. No human study in this set reports epilepsy patients with SLC17A8 variants, so "Established" is excluded and "Existing" is unlikely.

The only human genetic evidence is a single case report of a Kv4.2 (KCND2) N587fsX1 truncation mutation identified in one temporal lobe epilepsy patient, supported by electrophysiology showing reduced K+ current density (PMID 16934482); this is a single proband with no independent replication, so Established cannot be supported. A review of TLE genetics (PMID 19859879) merely cites this prior finding as background and adds no new probands. Remaining evidence is biological/expression-based: altered Kv4.2 expression in human epileptogenic focal lesions (PMID 19596445), and animal models of status epilepticus, kindling, and cortical malformation showing Kv4.2 dysregulation (PMIDs 18930118, 18727953, 17313824, 11517252), which support plausibility but are not human variant data. Other papers concern cardiac arrhythmia, blood pressure, or channel biophysics and are not relevant to an epilepsy variant association. Thus "Existing" is most likely, with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the single case report is considered insufficiently credible.

Two human genetic studies report positive associations of exonic LGI4 polymorphisms with epilepsy phenotypes: c.1914GC→AT with childhood absence epilepsy (PMID 14505228) and c.1722G/A with benign familial infantile convulsions (PMID 19815358), both small case-control studies of common variants rather than demonstrations of causal mutations. Against causality, a targeted screen of ADPEAF families found no LGI4 mutations (PMID 15079010), and the remaining literature is biological: LGI4 positional mapping to 19q13.11 (PMID 12023020), brain expression (PMIDs 19833108, 15857855), secretion/ADAM22 binding (PMID 20156119), and mouse claw paw/knockout peripheral nerve and gliogenesis phenotypes (PMIDs 16341215, 21068328) — none of which are human epilepsy-causing variants. No two papers report pathogenic LGI4 variants in independent probands/families, so Established cannot be supported. The human association data are credible but limited and unreplicated, which best fits "Existing," with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given that the strongest mechanistic evidence is animal/in vitro.

No human genetic study in this set implicates SV2B variants in epilepsy; the only candidate-gene association study explicitly found no association of SV2B (or SV2A/SV2C) polymorphisms with epilepsy predisposition or levetiracetam response (PMID 18977120). The supportive evidence is entirely animal/in vitro: SV2B knockout mice are phenotypically normal alone, but SV2A/SV2B double knockouts show severe seizures and death, implying functional redundancy (PMID 10624962), and SV2B loss alters presynaptic Ca2+ and neurotransmitter release in a manner proposed as a therapeutic target in epilepsy (PMID 20620874). Expression and vesicle-biology studies (PMIDs 8083732, 20053882, 21124874) and levetiracetam-binding work showing LEV binds SV2A but not SV2B (PMIDs 15210974, 16556440, 16434140) provide pathway relevance but no genetic evidence. The SV2B mention in a depression linkage/LD mapping paper (PMID 18367154) is unrelated to epilepsy. This profile best fits "Hypothesized."

The only available article (PMID 15760900) concerns stargazin, encoded by Cacng2, whose mutation causes epilepsy and ataxia in the "stargazer" mouse; CACNG1 is mentioned solely as one of eight paralogous Cacng family genes with no functional or genetic data linking it to seizures. There are no human genetic studies, no patient variants, and no probands or families implicating CACNG1, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The only conceivable support is indirect guilt-by-family-membership with a calcium-channel gamma subunit whose paralogue causes murine epilepsy, which is a very thin basis for Hypothesized. Because the co-mention is essentially incidental to a paper about Cacng2 and claudin-like adhesion, Novel is the most defensible call, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized given the shared gene family and calcium-channel/AMPA-receptor biology.

None of the provided articles reports CACNA1C variants identified in human epilepsy patients or families; the human genetic literature here concerns bipolar disorder/schizophrenia (rs1006737) and cardiac channelopathies (long QT/Timothy syndrome, short QT). The only direct epilepsy link is the stargazer mutant mouse, in which absence epilepsy and ataxia are accompanied by reduced cerebellar Cav1.2 (CACNA1C) protein — an animal/biological finding, not human genetic evidence (PMID 19422811). Ion-channel candidate-gene reviews co-mention CACNA1C with CNS hyperexcitability phenotypes and seizures in a speculative framework (PMID 16497276), and a 12p13.33 terminal deletion disrupting CACNA1C involves many genes and a non-epilepsy phenotype (PMID 19733267), which cannot isolate the gene. Thus the relationship is best described as biologically plausible (hypothesized), with only weak, indirect support for a human association.

The evidence here is entirely from animal models and in vitro work: alpha-CaMKII null mutant mice develop limbic/hippocampal seizures (PMID 7624331), antisense knockdown of CaMKII-alpha in cultured hippocampal neurons produces epileptiform discharges (PMID 10779547), and numerous rodent seizure models (kainate, pilocarpine, kindling, PTZ, penicillin) show altered CaMKII-alpha expression and dendritic mRNA targeting (PMIDs 9523577, 12121312, 14614906, 18710651, 19446251). Transgenic studies using the CaMKIIα promoter (PMIDs 11248115, 10103085) are promoter-driven tools, not evidence about the gene itself. The only human study (PMID 17855601) uses CaMKIIα merely as a pyramidal-cell marker in TLE tissue, with no genetic variant data. No human probands or families with CAMK2A variants are reported, so Established and Existing are not supported; the strong, mechanistically direct animal/cellular data make Hypothesized the correct category.

No article in this set reports variants in GABRR1 causing or associating with epilepsy itself. The only epilepsy-related study (PMID 16675198) examined GABRR1 as a candidate for vigabatrin-induced visual field constriction in epilepsy patients, and the initial SNP/haplotype correlations failed replication in a second cohort, so it is effectively a negative pharmacogenetic finding rather than evidence of an epilepsy association. The remaining genetic studies link GABRR1/GABRR2 to alcohol dependence, autism, and schizophrenia/bipolar disorder (PMIDs 19536785, 16080114, 20889312), phenotypes that are not recognized precursors or subtypes of epilepsy. However, GABRR1 encodes the rho1 subunit of GABA-gated chloride channels, and the functional/pharmacological work (PMIDs 18599601, 18385542, 1315307) establishes a direct biological link to inhibitory neurotransmission, the canonical mechanism of seizure control, supporting a "Hypothesized" relationship. A residual probability is assigned to Novel because no study here measures seizure phenotypes in relation to this gene, and to Existing because of the candidate-gene consideration of GABRR1 in an epilepsy cohort.

The direct human genetic studies in this set are negative: mutation screening of KCNJ6 in 38 JME patients found only synonymous changes (PMID 10686544), and an association study of IGE found no association for either KCNJ6 SNP, while a neighboring gene KCNJ3 showed suggestive signals (PMID 12458027). The chromosome 21q22 deletion cases with epilepsy (PMID 16418593) span many megabases and dozens of genes, so they cannot implicate KCNJ6 specifically. Strong supporting biology comes from animal and in vitro work: GIRK2 knockout mice show spontaneous and provoked seizures (PMID 9023358), weaver mice with a GIRK2 pore mutation show tonic-clonic seizures and altered hippocampal GABA-B/Kir3 signaling (PMIDs 12879981, 9592081), drug studies link GIRK inhibition to seizure side effects, and GIRK2/Kir3.2 is proposed as an anti-epileptic drug target (PMIDs 12504910, 17168757, 15542767). Human studies of KCNJ6 variants concern opioid response and nicotine dependence rather than epilepsy (PMIDs 20220551, 17135278). This profile fits "Hypothesized": compelling mechanistic and animal-model evidence without any positive human variant association.

The only evidence linking CLCN3 to epilepsy comes from mouse knockout work: Clcn3−/− mice display spontaneous seizures, progressive hippocampal/dentate degeneration, loss of GABA-synthesizing neurons and altered GABA(A) receptor expression (PMID 12470859), plus a broader neurodegenerative, NCL-like phenotype (PMID 12059962). These animal and biophysical data (ClC-3 as an intracellular Cl−/H+ transporter regulating vesicular acidification, PMIDs 17977943, 18853181) give strong biological plausibility for a role in neuronal excitability, but they are not human genetic evidence. Human-oriented studies here screened CLCN3 as a candidate and found no disease-causing variants (arRP family, PMID 11381043; canine late-onset NCL, PMID 16515703), and no human epilepsy cohort or proband with a CLCN3 variant is reported. Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with no basis for Established and only minimal weight for Existing.

The only direct human genetic study of GABRB2 in epilepsy (PMID 15955415) screened GABRA1, GABRB2 and GABRG2 in 52 Japanese patients with typical/atypical absence seizures and found only silent polymorphisms, explicitly concluding GABRB2 is not a major genetic cause. The other GABRB2 genetic papers concern schizophrenia and bipolar disorder (PMIDs 19909288, 19763268, 18715757, 18583979, 20221451, 17167345), which are not epilepsy precursors, and some are negative. Supporting biology is nonetheless strong but non-genetic/non-human: the β2N265S knock-in mouse shows β2-containing GABA-A receptors mediate loreclezole's anticonvulsant action (PMID 16882014), and β2 subunit expression changes occur in rodent seizure models and limbic epilepsy tissue (PMIDs 18554471, 18992345). Established and Existing are therefore not supported by any positive human variant study; Hypothesized best fits the pathway/animal-model evidence.

None of the provided articles examines epilepsy at all; they concern schizophrenia (PMIDs 17982252, 16172613), autism (16080114), and beta-amyloid-induced neuronal degeneration in rodent/cell models (16930428). No human genetic study reports GABRP variants in epilepsy probands or families, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only basis for any relationship is indirect biology: GABRP encodes a GABA-A receptor pi subunit, and GABA-A receptor subunit genes within the 5q cluster are implicated in neuropsychiatric phenotypes and GABAergic inhibitory signalling, which is mechanistically relevant to seizure susceptibility; the Abeta study shows regulated neuronal Gabrp expression but in vitro/animal only. Given that nothing in this literature connects GABRP to seizures or epilepsy, the evidence best supports Novel, with a substantial residual weight on Hypothesized because of the receptor's inhibitory neurotransmission biology.

The evidence linking CACNA1E (Cav2.3) to epilepsy in this corpus is entirely non-human or mechanistic: Cav2.3-knockout mice show reduced PTZ/kainate seizure susceptibility and resistance to excitotoxicity (PMID 17376845, 16963121), rat absence-epilepsy models show altered alpha1E expression (PMID 10208591), and SNPs in rat CACNA1E associate with seizure threshold in kindling models (PMID 20638246) — a rat, not human, genetic finding. The only human genetic association data here concern migraine (negative after correction; PMIDs 17727731, 18676988) and type 2 diabetes/insulin resistance in Pima Indians (PMID 17720895), neither of which is epilepsy. The Cav2.3–EFHC1 interaction relevant to juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (PMID 15845089) is a protein-interaction/pathway argument implicating EFHC1 variants, not CACNA1E variants in patients. No article reports CACNA1E variants in human epilepsy probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is barely supported; the strong biological and animal-model rationale places this firmly in Hypothesized.

The primary human evidence is a case-control association of the PDYN promoter 68-bp repeat (low-expression "L" alleles) with temporal lobe epilepsy, particularly in patients with a family history of seizures (PMID 11835385), supported by a positive meta-analysis of 591 cases/1117 controls (PMID 18334734) and a non-significant trend in familial lateral TLE (PMID 18355961). However, several replication attempts failed (PMIDs 15888540, 19066720), and the variant is a common susceptibility polymorphism rather than a causal mutation, so no study demonstrates causation in independent probands or families — ruling out "Established." Supporting biology (functional promoter allele altering PDYN expression, PMID 10646497; seizure-induced PDYN mRNA upregulation in rodent models, PMIDs 1347633, 7898641, 9179861) strengthens plausibility but is in vitro/animal and only supports "Hypothesized." The overall weight of credible but inconsistent human association data places this firmly in the "Existing" category.

The literature up to 2010 provides strong biological rationale but no human genetic variant data. KCC2 (SLC12A5) sets neuronal chloride gradients and determines whether GABA is inhibitory or excitatory (PMID 9930699), and targeted disruption in mice produces lethal spontaneous seizures (PMIDs 17715129, 11826289); a Drosophila KCC hypomorph shows seizure-like behavior (PMID 19884312). Human studies cited are expression/protein-level analyses in epileptic cortex and TLE hippocampectomies (PMIDs 20132297, 19210758), which show altered KCC2 levels but not sequence variants in probands or families. Mapping of SLC12A5 to 20q12–q13.1 is explicitly offered as a candidate-gene resource for future studies, not as evidence of association (PMID 11701957). With no reported patient variants, the relationship is best classified as Hypothesized, with a small allowance for Existing based on human downregulation data in epileptic tissue.

No article reports a pathogenic CHRNB3 variant identified in epilepsy patients; in fact, two human studies explicitly excluded linkage and found no mutations in CHRNB3 (and other nAChR subunit genes) in ADNFLE families (PMID 12195439, 17324557), so Established is untenable. The strongest positive human evidence is a linkage study of adolescent-onset idiopathic generalized epilepsy with a multipoint LOD of ~3.2 to a chromosome 8 region that merely encompasses CHRNB3, which is proposed only as a positional candidate without any variant identified (PMID 10205274) — region-level linkage cannot single out this gene from its neighbours, so this supports a hypothesis more than a demonstrated association. The remaining papers concern nicotine dependence and chromosome 8p neuropsychiatric candidacy (PMID 19564872, 19204725), which provide biological plausibility (brain nAChR subunit, same receptor family as the proven ADNFLE genes CHRNA4/CHRNB2) but no epilepsy variant data. Therefore the weight falls mainly on Hypothesized, with a substantial share for Existing given the human linkage signal, and a small residual for Novel because the direct tests were negative.

None of the provided articles mention epilepsy, seizures, or any neurological phenotype; they concern nucleoside transporter cloning, structure–function, tissue expression (liver, adipose, breast), and pharmacogenetics of gemcitabine/antiviral nucleoside analogues. The only human genetic variant studies (PMIDs 14978229, 18538445, 15456697) link SLC28A1 polymorphisms to nucleoside analogue transport and chemotherapy toxicity, not to epilepsy. A very weak indirect biological rationale exists because SLC28 transporters can modulate extracellular adenosine levels (PMID 17926640), and adenosine signalling is neuromodulatory, but no CNS expression or seizure data are presented. There is therefore no evidence of causality or association with epilepsy, and the co-mentions are incidental, supporting Novel with only a small allowance for a hypothesized adenosine-related mechanism.

No article reports KCNN1 (SK1) sequence variants in human patients with epilepsy; there are no probands, families, or association studies. The supporting evidence is entirely animal/in vitro: reduced SK1 protein in inferior colliculus neurons of the genetically epilepsy-prone rat (PMID 19254702), altered SK1 expression in pilocarpine-treated epileptic rats (PMID 20553876), and pharmacological SK-channel activation suppressing epileptiform bursting in hippocampal slices (PMID 16336949). Additional papers establish SK1 expression in hippocampus/neocortex and its molecular/biophysical properties (PMIDs 12427825, 15127180, 11267657, 11258935, 17142458), which is biologically relevant to neuronal excitability but not genetic evidence. The Down syndrome microarray paper (PMID 15068253) is incidental. This profile fits "Hypothesized": plausible mechanistic and animal-model links without human variant data.

No article reports ADORA3 sequence variants, polymorphisms, or genetic association testing in epilepsy patients or families, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The evidence is entirely pharmacological and mechanistic: A3 agonists modulate chemically induced seizures in mice (PMID 7774659), A3 agonists are inactive/pro-excitatory in audiogenic seizure models (PMID 10357250), 2-Cl-IB-MECA facilitates epileptiform discharges in immature rat hippocampal slices (PMID 15246113), and A3 activation desensitizes protective A1 receptor responses in rat hippocampus (PMID 8987783). The one human-tissue study (PMID 19721003) is a functional ex vivo experiment showing an A3 antagonist improves GABA(A) current stability in epileptic tissue — biologically relevant but not genetic variant evidence. The remaining papers concern cancer, COPD, IBD, dry eye, kidney disease, or receptor structure–function and are not epilepsy-relevant. This pattern fits Hypothesized: strong biological/pathway and animal-model plausibility without variant-level human data.

The only human genetic studies that directly test GAD1 in an epilepsy phenotype (pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy/seizures) explicitly EXCLUDE linkage or mutation of GAD1, mapping the disease instead to 5q31 (PMIDs 10978228, 9621518, 10908915, 16075246). The GAD1 missense mutation reported by Lynex et al. (15571623) causes autosomal recessive spastic cerebral palsy, not epilepsy. The remaining supportive material is immunological (anti-GAD autoantibodies in drug-resistant epilepsy, stiff-person syndrome, limbic encephalitis; PMIDs 12536283, 18687732, 2135382, 20499581) — protein-level autoimmunity rather than germline variation — plus rodent expression data showing phenytoin alters Gad1 (20404047); other GAD1 association studies concern schizophrenia, autism, bipolar disorder, alcoholism, not epilepsy. This gives strong biological plausibility (GABA synthesis, GAD as epilepsy-related autoantigen) without credible human variant-based association, which best fits "Hypothesized," with a small residual chance that the autoantibody/epilepsy link is counted as "Existing."

None of the provided articles report genetic variants in SLC32A1 (VGAT) in epilepsy patients or families; there is no linkage, association, or sequencing study. Instead, the evidence is entirely expression/functional: altered VGAT-positive terminal density in experimental and human cortical dysplasia (PMID 20477846, 20618425, 18615638, 17711980), VGAT regulation after kainate or pilocarpine seizures (PMID 14620876, 17503488, 16930566), induced GABAergic phenotype including VGAT in granule cells of epileptic rats (PMID 16049169), differential VGAT expression in inhibitory versus excitatory hippocampal neurons as a proposed therapeutic target (PMID 12558566), and VGAT modulation by anticonvulsant-related drugs (PMID 15488295). These data make the gene biologically relevant to GABAergic inhibition and seizure susceptibility but are largely rodent or descriptive human tissue work, not variant-based. Hence the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with only a small residual probability that an unrecognized human genetic report exists.

SLC1A6 encodes EAAT4, a neuronal glutamate transporter, and the literature provides strong mechanistic/biological links to seizures but no human genetic variant evidence. The human neocortical epilepsy study (PMID 17868051) shows reduced EAAT4 mRNA and protein at epileptic foci, which is expression data rather than variant-based association. Mouse models (betaIII spectrin/Spnb3 knockouts, PMIDs 20231455, 20371805) develop myoclonic seizures with reduced EAAT4, and reviews (PMID 10515165) explicitly note that no human genetic epilepsy has been attributed to glutamate transporters. Human genetic association studies of SLC1A6 exist only for schizophrenia (PMID 17221839), not epilepsy, so the evidence falls squarely in the "Hypothesized" category; no article demonstrates causal variants in epilepsy probands or families.

None of the supplied articles reports epilepsy phenotypes or epilepsy-associated variants in GABRG1; the genetic studies concern autism (PMID 16556609, 16080114, 18163449) and, in the autism association study, the significant signals were in GABRA4/GABRB1/GABRR2, not GABRG1. The chromosomal cases are large inversions/duplications spanning a multigene GABA-A receptor cluster, which cannot implicate GABRG1 specifically, and none relates to seizures. However, PMID 1321425 establishes GABRG1 as encoding the γ1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter receptor and the target of barbiturates and benzodiazepines, providing a direct biological/pathway rationale for a possible role in seizure susceptibility. That mechanistic plausibility, without any human epilepsy genetic data in this corpus, places the evidence mainly at "Hypothesized," with some weight on "Novel" since epilepsy is never mentioned.

No article reports GABRA6 variants in human epilepsy patients or families; the human genetic studies involving GABRA6 polymorphisms (1519T>C, Pro385Ser) concern alcohol dependence, dissocial alcoholism, craving, abdominal obesity/cortisol, and perceived parenting (PMIDs 10195814, 18616664, 12080446, 16402352), and the autism association study implicated GABRA4/GABRB1, not GABRA6 (PMID 16080114). The relationship to epilepsy is supported only by biology and animal/in vitro work: gabra6 knockout and mutant mice, altered α6-containing GABA-A receptor expression in epileptic/ataxic tottering and stargazer mice, and receptor gating/pharmacology studies invoking a lysine residue whose mutation in other subunits is linked to inherited epilepsy (PMIDs 10515160, 17614209, 17646167, 20109529, 16554486, 15950783). This pathway-level and rodent-model evidence makes GABRA6 a plausible epilepsy candidate but provides no human variant evidence, so "Hypothesized" is the best fit, with a small residual probability for "Existing" and "Novel".

The only article that directly addresses epilepsy with CACNA1S genotyping is the Spanish kindred with essential tremor, late-onset seizures and hypokalemic periodic paralysis (PMID 11034874), and its own result explicitly EXCLUDED the CACNL1A3/CACNA1S Arg528His mutation as the cause of the tremor or the epilepsy — negative, not supportive, evidence. All other papers concern hypokalemic periodic paralysis, thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, paramyotonia or malignant hyperthermia, phenotypes that are skeletal-muscle channelopathies and not recognized precursors or subtypes of epilepsy (PMIDs 15534250, 12548523, 19779499, 11353725, 20634695, 20861472). The only link to epilepsy is the speculative statement in reviews that understanding skeletal muscle channelopathies may eventually illuminate CNS channel diseases such as migraine and epilepsy (PMID 16195244), which is a generic pathway musing rather than evidence for CACNA1S itself (a gene expressed essentially in skeletal muscle). Hence no credible human genetic association exists in this literature; a small weight is kept for "Hypothesized" because of the generic voltage-gated calcium channel/excitability rationale.

No articles were provided linking SYNGR3 to epilepsy, so there is no evidence of variants in this gene causing or associating with epilepsy in humans as of 2010/12/31. Without any citations, neither "Established" nor "Existing" can be supported, since both require at least one credible human genetic study. A small amount of probability is reserved for "Hypothesized" because synaptogyrins are synaptic vesicle proteins whose biology is broadly relevant to neuronal excitability, but no supporting literature is present here. The absence of any co-mention or functional report makes "Novel" the most appropriate designation.

Every article in this set concerns SCN4A (Nav1.4) in skeletal muscle channelopathies — hyperkalemic/hypokalemic/normokalemic periodic paralysis, paramyotonia congenita, potassium-aggravated myotonia and a congenital myasthenic syndrome — with no report of epilepsy or seizures in SCN4A mutation carriers. Epilepsy appears only incidentally: PMID 15774523 draws an analogy to GEFS+ caused by C-terminal mutations in *other* Nav channels (SCN1A/SCN1B), and PMID 16195244 speculates that understanding muscle channelopathies may eventually inform common CNS channel diseases such as migraine and epilepsy. These are background remarks, not evidence that SCN4A variants contribute to epilepsy. No human study here reports a proband or family in which an SCN4A variant segregates with seizures (the "cyanotic attacks" in PMID 19347921 are myotonic, not epileptic). The only reason not to assign all weight to Novel is the weak biological analogy with paralogous neuronal sodium channels in which gating defects cause epilepsy, which supports a modest Hypothesized allocation.

Human genetic evidence exists: Escayg et al. (PMID 10762541) report the R482X truncating mutation in a juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patient and the C104F missense variant in a German family with generalized epilepsy with praxis-induced seizures, absent from 510 control chromosomes, with modest functional effects in oocytes. A second independent human study (PMID 18755274) identified an inherited CACNB4 R468Q variant in an SCN1A-mutation-positive SMEI proband whose father had febrile seizures, with electrophysiological evidence of increased Cav2.1 currents, but frames it as a genetic modifier rather than a primary cause. Supporting biology is strong but non-human: the lethargic (Cacnb4lh) mouse model of absence epilepsy and related functional studies (PMIDs 9628818, 10407181, 10322048, 10515159). Several human studies excluded CACNB4 in CAE, JME, migrainous vertigo, and EA cohorts (PMIDs 20561025, 20378313, 16866717, 20129625), indicating the evidence is limited and not robustly replicated, so "Existing" is the best fit, with some weight on "Established" given two independent patient-based reports.

Two human studies from the same group report linkage (HLOD 3.54) and transmission disequilibrium for SNPs in the 5'UTR/exon 1 region of CACNG3 in childhood absence epilepsy families and trios (PMID 17264864), building on earlier suggestive linkage at the CACNG3 locus (PMID 11904235). However, re-sequencing identified no coding or clearly causal variants, and the authors themselves frame CACNG3 as a susceptibility locus in only a subset of patients rather than a causative gene. No independent replication in separate cohorts or families with identified pathogenic variants is presented, so the "Established" criterion (at least two papers with causal variants in independent probands) is not met. The evidence is human, genetic, and association-level, which fits "Existing" best, with a modest residual probability that the signal reflects only biological plausibility (calcium channel subunit) rather than a confirmed association.

None of the provided articles report SYT2 variants in human patients with epilepsy; there are no probands, families, or association studies, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The strongest functional data are from a mouse carrying an I377N substitution in synaptotagmin 2, which causes severe ataxia with impaired Ca2+-triggered and increased spontaneous neurotransmitter release at brainstem synapses (PMID 16642042), and calyx of Held work showing synaptotagmin's role in vesicle positioning and synchronous release (PMID 19709630) — relevant excitability biology, but no seizure phenotype. The electroconvulsive seizure study (PMID 18563845) examines synaptic vesicle proteins in a rat seizure model but implicates synaptotagmin III, not SYT2, so it is at best a weak, indirect co-mention. Remaining papers concern biochemistry (Ca2+ binding, oligomerization, botulinum toxin receptor function, WNK1 phosphorylation, mucin secretion) with no epilepsy link, supporting a plausible but unproven mechanistic hypothesis rather than genetic evidence.

The only human genetic evidence is the EPIGEN multicentre case-control study (PMID 17913586), which reported KCNMB4 among five genes emerging from set-association analysis, but explicitly stated no clear, replicated risk variants were identified and that the tentative associations require confirmation in independent cohorts. This is a credible but limited single human association study, fitting "Existing" rather than "Established" (no independent probands/families with causal variants in KCNMB4 itself). Supporting biology is strong but indirect: the epilepsy/dyskinesia-causing mutation is in the pore-forming alpha subunit (KCNMA1), with beta4 only modulating its gating in vitro (PMID 19204046), and beta4 (KCNMB4) is highly brain-enriched and alters BK channel pharmacology (PMID 10792058). The cochlea and parotid expression papers (PMID 12454985, 12388098) are peripheral tissue expression data only. Thus the weight falls between Existing (one tentative human association) and Hypothesized (brain-expressed BK subunit with disease-relevant channel biology).

None of the provided articles mention epilepsy, seizures, or any seizure-related phenotype; they concern ADORA2B cloning/chromosomal mapping, receptor pharmacology (constitutive activity, inverse agonists, desensitization), endothelial hypoxia signaling, zebrafish development/Parkinson models, and adenosine receptor expression in an HPRT-knockout mouse (where ADORA2B expression was explicitly unchanged). There are no human genetic association studies, no patient variants, and no animal seizure models linking ADORA2B to epilepsy, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A modest allocation to Hypothesized reflects only the general biological plausibility that adenosine receptor signaling in the CNS (PMIDs 16793031, 19070682) could relate to neuronal excitability, but even this is indirect and not framed around epilepsy in any of these papers. On this literature alone the relationship is essentially unexamined, favoring Novel.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant in NT5E in patients with epilepsy, nor any association study linking NT5E to seizures. The epilepsy-related papers (PMIDs 7084136, 19440746) concern the cholesterol synthesis/trafficking inhibitor U18666A and an absence-epilepsy animal model, with no mention of NT5E. The NT5E papers concern oral cancer expression profiling, coeliac disease mucosal expression, thiopurine cytotoxicity pharmacogenomics, and endothelial–neutrophil adenosine generation — none involving epilepsy. The only tenuous biological bridge is that CD73/NT5E generates extracellular adenosine, and adenosine signalling is noted to influence neurotransmission (PMIDs 16799190, 12838422), which gives a weak, indirect mechanistic rationale but no epilepsy-specific data; hence most weight goes to Novel with a residual share for Hypothesized.

The only primary human genetic evidence linking SLC1A3 to seizures is Jen et al. (PMID 16116111), reporting a single de novo heterozygous EAAT1 mutation in one proband with episodic ataxia, seizures, hemiplegic migraine, with functional data showing reduced glutamate uptake and a dominant-negative effect. The second mutation-positive family (PMID 19139306, C186S) had episodic ataxia explicitly WITHOUT seizures, so it does not constitute a replicated epilepsy proband; other screens were negative (PMID 17236110) or found no SLC1A3 mutations (PMID 17645764, 19372292), and the review (PMID 20495966) merely restates the known case as background. Thus the criterion of two independent epilepsy probands/families is not met, precluding "Established." Substantial supporting biology exists but is non-human or non-genetic: GLAST knockout mice show high seizure susceptibility (PMID 12225864), GLAST downregulation in iron-induced and genetic rodent epilepsy models (PMIDs 10648893, 10771246, 11953453, 19853022), and altered transporter expression in human sclerotic hippocampus (PMID 17112731), which alone would support only "Hypothesized."

One human case-control genetic association study directly tests CYP2D6 variants (100C>T and 2850C>T) against generalized tonic clonic seizures in an Indian cohort and reports a significant association for 2850C>T (PMID 16835697), which meets the bar for "Existing". A review (PMID 10319191) restates that CYP2D6 polymorphism has been associated with risk of several disorders including epilepsy, but this is background citation rather than independent primary evidence, so it cannot establish replication. The remaining literature concerns CYP2D6-mediated metabolism of drugs whose toxicity or interactions can precipitate seizures (fluoxetine, venlafaxine/trimipramine, clomipramine, propafenone, hydrocodone, dextromethorphan in NKH), which supports a biological/pharmacological link to drug-induced seizures rather than epilepsy causation; notably one study genotyping patients with antidepressant-associated seizures found no poor metabolizers (PMID 9395157). Since only a single primary human association study exists without independent replication, "Established" is not supportable, and residual probability is assigned to "Hypothesized" given the mechanistic/pharmacogenetic rationale.

No article here reports KCNC1 variants in patients with epilepsy; the only human mutation screening (USH1C candidate gene analysis, PMID 9041816/9445488) found no coding mutations and concerns deafness, not epilepsy. The evidence connecting KCNC1 to epilepsy is purely biological/mechanistic: Kv3.1 channels shape fast-spiking interneuron firing and action potential repolarization, the antiepileptic drug levetiracetam inhibits Kv3.1-encoded delayed-rectifier current (PMID 20065495), and Kv3 subunits are implicated in the 4-aminopyridine model of ictogenesis in chronic epileptic rats (PMID 17942314). Notably, the Kcnc1-null mouse does not show spontaneous seizures (PMID 9037088), weakening but not eliminating the plausibility. Related family member Kv3.3 (KCNC3) causes SCA13, not epilepsy. Therefore "Hypothesized" best fits, with some residual weight on "Novel" given the negative mouse seizure phenotype.

The great majority of the evidence here is non-human or non-genetic: HCN1 knockout mice show increased seizure susceptibility and severity (PMIDs 19726656, 20384728), rat absence models (WAG/Rij, GAERS) show inherited or acquired loss/alteration of HCN1 expression (PMIDs 15182313, 17095562, 16251434, 16728450), and seizure models show transcriptional downregulation of HCN1 (PMIDs 12040066, 17964174, 15504329, 18397293). Human data consist mainly of altered I(H)/HCN1 biophysics in resected epileptogenic neocortex (PMID 19694789), which is expression/function, not variant evidence. The only human genetic study is the mutation screen of HCN1/HCN2 in 84 IGE patients (PMID 17931874), which reported a single HCN1 A881T substitution in one sporadic patient absent from 510 controls, with no functional validation and an explicit caveat that the contribution remains unclear — a single, limited, unreplicated finding. That supports at most "Existing" and cannot support "Established," since no two independent human studies with HCN1 variants in probands/families exist in this literature.

The only epilepsy-relevant article (PMID 16876319) screened GSTA4 as a positional candidate in the EJM1 region of chromosome 6p12 in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients and explicitly excluded it: no significant or potentially functional mutations were found, with EFHC1 identified as the causal gene instead. All other listed papers concern GSTA4 enzymology (4-hydroxynonenal conjugation, crystal structures), xenobiotic metabolism, skin and liver cancer susceptibility, docetaxel clearance, or ethanol preference in rats — none addresses epilepsy. A general oxidative-stress/detoxification role could offer a tenuous biological rationale (4-HNE detoxification in brain), which keeps some weight on Hypothesized, but no expression or model data specifically link GSTA4 to seizures. Therefore the evidence as of 2010 is essentially negative/incidental, favoring Novel.

The strongest evidence is from mouse models: a hypomorphic retroviral insertion in Gria4 underlies spike-wave discharges in C3H/HeJ mice, and Gria4 knockouts show absence seizures (PMID 18316356), with further characterization of SWD development and strain genetics (PMIDs 19409755, 19170754). These are animal, not human, genetic data, so they support "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing". Human studies here report altered GluR4 (GRIA4) mRNA/protein expression in refractory epilepsy, cortical dysplasia, hemimegalencephaly, and WAG/Rij rats (PMIDs 9455976, 11294928, 15571509, 16487682), which is expression/biology rather than variant evidence. The only human variant-type data is a BAC array-CGH study where GRIA4 falls within multi-gene copy number changes in mentally retarded children (PMID 19623214), which cannot isolate GRIA4 and does not test epilepsy specifically. No human study reports epilepsy-causing GRIA4 variants in probands or families, so Established is essentially excluded.

Only one article in this set addresses epilepsy at all (PMID 20064729), and it explicitly reports no significant association between UGT (along with CYP2C9/CYP2C19) polymorphisms and antiepileptic drug resistance; the only signals found were for ABCB1. No article reports UGT2B7 variants causing or being associated with epilepsy itself in any proband or family, so Established is excluded and Existing is barely supportable. The remaining literature concerns UGT2B7 biochemistry, glucuronidation of morphine, mycophenolate, steroids and bile acids, hepatotoxicity, and breast cancer — relevant to drug metabolism generally but not to epileptogenesis. A weak biological rationale exists (UGT2B7 glucuronidates antiepileptic drugs, hence candidate-gene testing in epilepsy pharmacogenetics), which supports Hypothesized over Novel, though the tested association was negative.

None of the provided articles mentions epilepsy, seizures, or any epilepsy-related phenotype, and none reports STX3 variants in patients. The bulk of the literature concerns STX3/syntaxin 3 as a t-SNARE in polarized epithelial trafficking (kidney, MDCK, Caco-2, RPE, prostate), aquaporin and amylase secretion, and Munc18b binding (PMIDs 16785322, 12198139, 10788461, 19515809, 17442889, 20695848, 12414999), which is irrelevant to seizure biology. A minority of papers place syntaxin-3 in neural/synaptic contexts — synaptic membrane expansion and synaptogenesis with DHA/uridine, changes after fluid percussion brain injury, and SNARE-mediated neurotransmitter exocytosis (PMIDs 19262950, 20816821, 11193390) — providing only a generic, indirect mechanistic rationale (synaptic vesicle fusion) that could support a weak "hypothesized" reading. There is no human genetic evidence of any kind, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded; the evidence here is best described as incidental co-mention with at most a speculative pathway link.

None of the provided articles mentions epilepsy or seizures at all. The yeast GLS2 paper (PMID 9430631) concerns a glucosidase II gene in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and is a homonym, not the human glutaminase 2 gene. The genome-wide interaction statistic paper (PMID 20885795) reports GLS2 SNP interactions in psoriasis, an unrelated phenotype, and the schizophrenia study (PMID 17669570) explicitly found no association of GLS/GLS2 with schizophrenia. The only tenuous basis for a link is the general role of glutaminase in glutamatergic neurotransmission, which could support a weak "hypothesized" biological rationale, but no epilepsy-relevant expression, pathway, or animal model data are presented here. Therefore the evidence as of 2010 is essentially absent, favoring Novel with some weight to Hypothesized.

The only human genetic association studies in this set that genotyped TNF variants (PMID 20486195, TNFA promoter in febrile seizures; PMID 19055487, TNFA -1037C/T in febrile seizures) both reported no significant association, with positive findings instead for IL-1Ra and IL-10. No paper reports TNF variants in epilepsy probands or families, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported by positive human genetic data. However, there is substantial biological evidence linking TNF to seizures: TNF-α is overexpressed in experimental seizure models and modulates neuronal excitability (PMID 18495419), CSF TNF-α is elevated in children during febrile convulsions and bacterial meningitis with seizures (PMIDs 11380915, 2355190), soluble TNF receptor levels track with seizure-associated encephalopathies (PMIDs 17597322, 19114298, 15207249), and recombinant TNF infusion in patients caused seizures as a dose-limiting toxicity (PMIDs 1428728, 2642024). This pattern—relevant mechanism and expression data without supportive variant evidence—fits "Hypothesized," with a small residual probability for "Existing" given the borderline cytokine/seizure-susceptibility literature.

None of the provided articles examine epilepsy or seizure phenotypes, and none report ABCC10/MRP7 variants in patients with epilepsy; all are about multidrug resistance in cancer cells, transporter genomic structure, or expression in leukemia. The only tenuous biological link is the general statement that MRP-family transporters at the blood–brain barrier can restrict drug penetration into the CNS (PMIDs 18220559, 22504741), a mechanism sometimes invoked for pharmacoresistance, but ABCC10 is not specifically tied to epilepsy here. Functional data in this set are in vitro (HEK293, MDCK) or murine (PMID 11943485), so no human genetic evidence exists to support Existing or Established. Accordingly, the evidence base is essentially incidental co-mention, favoring Novel with a modest allowance for a weakly hypothesized BBB-efflux rationale.

The ADRB2-specific articles concern spontaneous preterm birth (PMID 17267840), NNK-induced pulmonary adenocarcinoma in hamsters (PMID 15942941), and autism risk in the AGRE cohort (PMID 17199132) — none address epilepsy or seizure phenotypes. The epilepsy-related articles (e.g., PMIDs 17326542, 1794357, 181242, 2446831, 10962053) are animal seizure models, EEG/mapping studies, or clinical/behavioral reports that never mention ADRB2 and in several cases involve the homonym "bar" (bar pressing, lightbar, bar chewing, Bar-On EQ-i, Bar Harbor) rather than the gene. There is thus no genetic, expression, pathway, or model evidence linking ADRB2 variation or biology to epilepsy in this corpus; the co-mentions are incidental. A small residual probability is retained for a weak biological rationale via catecholamine/adrenergic signaling in brain development mentioned in the autism paper.

The only article linking STX7 to epilepsy-related phenotypes is the mapping of a pure simple febrile seizure locus to 6q22-q24 (PMID 12429594), where syntaxin 7 was examined as a positional/functional candidate but was explicitly EXCLUDED by sequence analysis — i.e., negative evidence rather than support for association. No study reports epilepsy-associated variants in STX7 in patients or families, so Established and Existing are unsupported. The remaining papers concern schizophrenia candidate-gene testing (also negative for STX7, PMID 18198266), endosome fusion biology (PMID 19032933), and neutrophil syntaxin expression (PMID 10080545), none of which address seizure mechanisms. A modest weight is retained for Hypothesized because STX7 is a SNARE involved in membrane/vesicle trafficking and was selected as a candidate "based on function" within a febrile seizure locus, giving a weak biological rationale; otherwise the co-mentions are incidental, favoring Novel.

No study in this set reports a CHRNA6 variant found in epilepsy patients; on the contrary, two human linkage/mutation studies in ADNFLE families explicitly excluded CHRNA6 along with other nAChR subunit genes (PMID 12195439, PMID 17324557). The strongest supportive material is biological/positional: CHRNA6 belongs to the nAChR family in which CHRNA4, CHRNB2 and CHRNA2 mutations cause ADNFLE, and it maps to 8p11.21-11.22, the putative region for adolescent-onset idiopathic generalized epilepsy (PMID 12406580). Other papers concern nicotine dependence, zebrafish expression, mouse RFLP/nicotine sensitivity, or 8p neuropsychiatric gene reviews, which are non-human or non-epilepsy evidence and support only a hypothesized link (PMIDs 19564872, 19301390, 11927835, 19204725). Therefore the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with a meaningful chance of being considered novel given the explicit exclusion results.

The strongest evidence is biological/functional rather than genetic: RLIP76 is overexpressed in membranes from excised epileptic foci, transports phenytoin and carbamazepine in reconstituted liposomes, and RLIP76-/- knockout mice show dramatic phenytoin toxicity (PMID 16188027), supporting a mechanistic hypothesis for drug-resistant epilepsy. However, the two human genetic studies explicitly tested common RALBP1/RLIP76 variants and were negative: no association with AED response or with epilepsy susceptibility in 783 patients vs 359 controls (PMID 17437410), and no significant association across 13 tagging SNPs in 503 SANAD patients (PMID 18086001), with only a non-corrected subgroup signal in carbamazepine-treated patients. A review merely lists RLIP76/RALBP1 among candidate transporter genes as background (PMID 20648993), which is citation rather than evidence. Remaining articles concern cancer, Ral signaling, or thrombosis and are irrelevant to epilepsy. Hence the relationship is best described as hypothesized, with only a small residual chance of "existing" based on the weak carbamazepine subgroup finding.

The only primary human genetic evidence is a single large Italian pedigree with sleep-related epilepsy (nocturnal wandering and ictal fear) in which a heterozygous CHRNA2 I279N missense mutation co-segregated and showed increased ACh sensitivity in vitro (PMID 16826524); a follow-up functional study confirmed gain-of-function and altered pharmacology but adds no new patients (PMID 19383498). Attempts at replication were uniformly negative: no CHRNA2 mutations in 47 ADNFLE families (PMID 17602836), none in 46 Italian NFLE patients (PMID 18226955), none in 33 sporadic NFLE cases (PMID 19058950), and linkage to the CHRNA2 region was excluded in several ADNFLE families (PMIDs 12195439, 17324557). Reviews (PMIDs 17662253, 20832659) merely restate the single family as background, which does not constitute independent replication. Since only one proband/family demonstrates the causal variant in humans, the evidence is credible but limited, fitting "Existing" rather than "Established."
